new_statements.quote: Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists. Where stress deviates from the normal pattern or where stress may be unclear due to double vocoids, etc., it is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey-wide transcription convention: stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is left unmarked; a preceding apostrophe marks deviations or unclear cases. Applied to the Sarudu list (Jan 1983, C. Grimes, one informant): 49 rows of ~4 forms each are unmarked (= penultimate by convention); four forms carry a mark, three of them on the first syllable of a three-vowel word ('lařana 'road', 'řapai 'when', 'baika 'good' -- antepenultimate unless the vowel sequence is a diphthong, which is exactly the 'double vocoids' case the convention flags) and one on the penult (mořo'lo? 'far'). So: penultimate by default, with a handful of marked initial-stress or vowel-sequence forms.
new_statements.exceptions: The four marked Sarudu forms above; the convention itself names 'double vocoids' as a source of unclear stress. Antepenultimate exceptions are listed explicitly only for Selayar (p. 96), not for Sarudu.
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a survey wordlist. The sentence is an areal generalisation over all languages of the then South Sulawesi province (which includes Kaili-Pamona Sarudu), not a Sarudu-specific description; the Sarudu informant was not born of Sarudu parents (footnote 2) and Friberg & Laskowske 1989 and Valkama 1987 note his list sits closer to Kaili than the Nunu' dialect. No grammar or phonology of Sarudu exists; the only other first-hand data (Yamaguchi & Nakashima 2003 ELPR wordlist) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Grimes & Grimes' Sarudu (SAR) list was taken in January 1983 by C. Grimes from one informant (Abdurrachman P., 60, not born of Sarudu parents but raised in a Sarudu village); Valkama 1987:106 and Friberg & Laskowske 1989:11 report that this list is closer to Kaili and only 82-86% similar to the Nunu' and Kulu (Lariang) lists, so it may represent a coastal/Kaili-leaning variety rather than the Nunu' dialect. Same language as saru1242 (no separate glottocodes for the Nunu'/Kulu dialects). The stress sentence is phrased for 'South Sulawesi languages' in the geographic sense of the 1983 survey (all languages of the then province), which includes Kaili-Pamona Sarudu; it is not specific to the South Sulawesi genetic group.

sources.note: p. 94: stress in the surveyed South Sulawesi languages 'usually occurs on the penultimate syllable', is left unmarked in the word lists, and is marked with a preceding apostrophe only where it deviates or is unclear (double vocoids). The Sarudu rows carry four explicit marks, checked on the page images: p.145 ['lařana] 'road', p.177 ['řapai] 'when', p.179 [mořo'lo?] 'far', p.199 ['baika] 'good'; five other scanned apostrophes (pp. 119, 121, 157, 165, 185) are diacritic artefacts. The Sarudu entry itself (p. 59) gives only classification, 4,000 speakers, location, religion; no prosodic remark.
